"Distributed System": "A collection of independent computing nodes that coordinate over a network to appear and function as a single coherent system to end users. Such systems must contend with challenges including network latency, partial failures, and asynchronous communication.",
"Network Latency": "The time delay incurred when messages travel between nodes across a network, affecting the responsiveness and coordination of distributed components. It is a fundamental constraint that influences the design of distributed protocols and consistency guarantees.",
"Failure": "An event in which a node, process, or network link ceases to function correctly, potentially causing data loss, unavailability, or inconsistent behavior. Distributed systems must detect and tolerate various failure modes to remain operational.",
"Asynchrony": "The property of a distributed system in which messages may be delayed arbitrarily and nodes operate without a shared global clock or bounded response times. Asynchrony complicates coordination and necessitates specialized protocols for agreement.",
"Consensus Algorithm": "A protocol that enables a group of distributed nodes to agree on a single value or sequence of operations despite failures and asynchronous communication. Examples include Paxos and Raft, which underpin many replicated state machines.",
"Raft": "A consensus algorithm designed for understandability that achieves agreement among distributed nodes through leader election, log replication, and safety guarantees. It is widely used to implement fault-tolerant replicated services.",
"State Agreement": "The process by which multiple nodes in a distributed system converge on the same view of system state, typically achieved through a consensus algorithm. It ensures consistent decision-making across replicas.",
"Replication": "The practice of maintaining copies of data or services on multiple nodes to improve availability, durability, and fault tolerance. Replication strategies vary in how updates are propagated and synchronized among replicas.",
"Availability": "The degree to which a system remains operational and responsive to client requests, typically measured as the fraction of time service is accessible. Replication and redundancy are common techniques to increase availability.",
"Fault Tolerance": "The ability of a system to continue operating correctly in the presence of component failures, achieved through redundancy, replication, and recovery mechanisms. It is a core goal of distributed system design.",
"Partitioning": "The division of a dataset or workload across multiple nodes so that each node is responsible for a subset, enabling scalability and parallelism. Also called sharding, it must be balanced against concerns of consistency and routing.",
"Node": "An individual computing entity, such as a server or process, that participates in a distributed system by storing data, executing computations, or communicating with peers. Nodes are the basic units that collectively provide system functionality.",
"Data Distribution": "The strategy by which data is allocated and spread across the nodes of a distributed system, often through partitioning or replication. It affects performance, scalability, and fault tolerance characteristics.",
"Consistency Model": "A formal specification of the guarantees a distributed system provides regarding the visibility and ordering of updates across replicas. Different models trade off between stronger correctness guarantees and better performance or availability.",
"Safety": "A correctness property asserting that nothing bad happens, such as no two nodes committing conflicting values or exposing invalid state. In consistency models, safety typically constrains the set of allowable system behaviors.",
"Performance": "A measure of system efficiency, typically expressed in terms of throughput, latency, and resource utilization. Consistency and fault tolerance mechanisms often impose performance trade-offs in distributed systems.",
"Strong Consistency": "A consistency model in which all nodes observe updates in the same order and reads reflect the most recent write, providing the illusion of a single, up-to-date data store. It offers strong guarantees at the cost of latency and availability.",
"Eventual Consistency": "A relaxed consistency model guaranteeing that, in the absence of new updates, all replicas will eventually converge to the same state. It permits temporary divergence among replicas in exchange for higher availability and lower latency.",
"Update Visibility": "The property describing when and to whom modifications to data become observable across a distributed system. Different consistency models provide different guarantees about the timing and ordering of update visibility.",
"Temporary Divergence": "A state in which replicas of the same data hold differing values for a limited period before converging, typically under eventual consistency. Such divergence is tolerated to improve availability and performance."
}
